prompt: A reference frame is inertial when:

options.t: Newton's laws hold in it, and a force-free body moves at constant velocity
It is at rest relative to the centre of the universe
options.why: Relativity does not privilege a fixed absolute frame; inertial frames move uniformly relative to one another.

options.t: It rotates at a constant angular speed
options.why: A rotating frame is generally non-inertial because fictitious forces are needed to describe motion.

options.t: It is attached to any accelerating object
options.why: An accelerating frame is non-inertial in the usual Newtonian description.

explain: An inertial frame is one in which Newton's first law holds: a body with no net force remains at rest or moves uniformly in a straight line.

prompt: Which statement is one of Einstein's special-relativity postulates?

options.t: The laws of physics have the same form in all inertial frames
The laws of mechanics apply only in the frame where a body starts
options.why: The postulate applies to all inertial frames, not one preferred starting frame.

options.t: Absolute rest can be detected by measuring light in one direction
options.why: Special relativity has no preferred inertial frame in which absolute motion can be measured.

options.t: Time is absolute and independent of the observer
options.tag: Used the Newtonian view of time
options.why: In special relativity, measurements of time and simultaneity can depend on the inertial observer.

explain: Einstein's first postulate states that all laws of physics are the same in every inertial reference frame. His second postulate states that light in vacuum has the same speed for all inertial observers.

prompt: Frame K' moves at speed v in the positive x direction relative to K. What is the Galilean coordinate transformation for x'?

options.why: For K' moving in the positive direction, subtract its displacement vt from x to obtain x'.
The gamma factor belongs to the Lorentz transformation, not the Galilean transformation.
The displacement of the moving frame is vt, not v/t.

explain: For the stated direction of motion, the Galilean transformation is x'=x-vt. It also assumes t'=t; the inverse relation is x=x'+vt.

prompt: What is the Lorentz factor for an object moving at 0.8c?

options.why: gamma=1/sqrt(1-v^2/c^2), so it is greater than one for nonzero speed.
The expression uses the square of v/c: gamma=1/sqrt(1-v^2/c^2).
gamma approaches one only when v is much smaller than c.

prompt: A spaceship has a proper length of 10 m and passes an observer at 0.8c. What length does that observer measure along the direction of motion?

options.why: The moving length parallel to the motion is L=L0/gamma, which is shorter than its proper length.

options.tag: Multiplied instead of divided by gamma
options.why: Length contraction divides the proper length by gamma.
Length contraction uses 1/gamma=sqrt(1-v^2/c^2), not 1-v/c.

explain: At 0.8c, gamma=5/3. The measured length is L=L0/gamma=10/(5/3)=6 m.

prompt: A clock measures 2.0 s between two events that occur at the same place in the clock's rest frame. How much time elapses according to an observer for whom the clock moves at 0.8c?

options.tag: Applied length contraction to a time interval
options.why: The moving clock runs slow: the observer measures the dilated interval gamma times the proper time.
The interval measured in the clock's rest frame is the proper time; a moving observer measures a longer interval.

options.tag: Reported gamma instead of elapsed time
options.why: Multiply the proper time, 2.0 s, by gamma=5/3.

explain: The proper time is 2.0 s and gamma=5/3, so the moving observer measures Delta t=gamma Delta tau=(5/3)(2.0)=10/3 s.

prompt: Two events are simultaneous in one inertial frame. Which statement is generally correct?

options.t: They need not be simultaneous in a frame moving relative to the first
They are simultaneous in every inertial frame
options.why: Relativity of simultaneity means observers in relative motion can disagree about whether separated events occurred at the same time.

options.t: They become simultaneous only if both occur at the same position
options.why: The events can be spatially separated; simultaneity can still depend on the frame.

options.t: Their order is reversed in every moving frame
options.why: Relativity permits different time assignments for separated events, but does not require a reversal in every frame.

explain: For spatially separated events, simultaneity depends on the inertial frame. Observers in relative motion can disagree about whether the events occurred at the same time.

prompt: When is the Galilean transformation a good approximation to the Lorentz transformation?

options.t: When the relative speed is much smaller than the speed of light
Only when the relative speed equals the speed of light
options.why: The Galilean limit is v/c much less than one, not v=c.

options.t: When the moving frame accelerates rapidly
options.why: The approximation concerns relative speed compared with c; an accelerating frame is a separate issue.

options.t: At every speed if the time coordinates are set equal
options.tag: Assumed absolute time at relativistic speeds
options.why: At speeds approaching c, Lorentz time and space transformations cannot generally be replaced by Galilean ones.

explain: For v much smaller than c, gamma is approximately one and the Lorentz transformations reduce to the Galilean transformations.

prompt: What is the relativistic momentum of a particle with rest mass m and speed v?

options.why: Relativistic momentum is gamma times the Newtonian expression mv.
Momentum has units of mass times speed; total energy is gamma mc^2.
Momentum is proportional to velocity, not velocity squared.

explain: The relativistic momentum is p=gamma mv, with gamma=1/sqrt(1-v^2/c^2). At low speed gamma approaches one and p approaches mv.

prompt: A particle moves at 0.6c. What is its relativistic momentum in terms of its rest mass m?

options.why: At 0.6c the Lorentz factor is 1.25, so p=gamma m(0.6c).
The momentum also includes the speed factor 0.6c.
Relativistic momentum uses gamma, not its reciprocal.

explain: gamma=1/sqrt(1-0.6^2)=1.25. Therefore p=gamma mv=1.25m(0.6c)=0.75mc.

prompt: Which expression gives a particle's total relativistic energy?

options.why: gamma mv is relativistic momentum; total energy has units and form gamma mc^2.
Rest energy is mc^2, not mc.
(gamma-1)mc^2 is relativistic kinetic energy; total energy also includes rest energy.

explain: The total energy is E=gamma mc^2. At rest gamma=1, so the energy is the rest energy E0=mc^2.

prompt: A particle moves at 0.6c. What is its kinetic energy in terms of its rest energy mc^2?

options.why: The total energy is 1.25mc^2; subtract the rest energy mc^2 to get kinetic energy.
Relativistic kinetic energy is (gamma-1)mc^2, not (v/c)mc^2.
The exact relativistic kinetic energy uses gamma-1, not v^2/c^2.

explain: For v=0.6c, gamma=1.25. Thus K=(gamma-1)mc^2=0.25mc^2.

prompt: What is the relativistic kinetic energy of a particle at rest?

options.t: Zero; its total energy is still mc^2

options.tag: Confused rest energy with kinetic energy
options.why: Rest energy is part of total energy, but kinetic energy is zero when the particle is at rest.

options.t: gamma mc^2 with gamma equal to zero
options.why: At rest gamma=1, not zero.

options.tag: Applied the light-speed limit at rest
options.why: The Lorentz factor is finite and equals one when v=0.

explain: K=(gamma-1)mc^2. At rest v=0 and gamma=1, so K=0 while total energy remains E0=mc^2.

prompt: Which idealized property defines a blackbody?

options.t: It absorbs all incident radiation and reflects none

options.why: A blackbody is an ideal absorber, not a perfect reflector.

options.t: It emits radiation at one wavelength only
options.tag: Confused a spectrum with a spectral line
options.why: A blackbody emits a continuous spectrum whose distribution depends on temperature.

options.t: Its radiation depends on the chemical material of the cavity
options.why: At thermal equilibrium, the blackbody spectrum is universal and independent of the cavity material.

explain: A blackbody is an ideal absorber: it absorbs all radiation incident on it and reflects none. In thermal equilibrium it is also an excellent emitter.

prompt: Why is a small opening into a hollow cavity a useful approximation to a blackbody?

options.t: Radiation entering the opening is repeatedly reflected inside and is very likely to be absorbed
The opening emits only the light originally reflected from its surface
options.why: Repeated internal reflections make the entering radiation unlikely to escape before being absorbed.

options.t: The cavity makes all incident radiation change to a single frequency
options.why: The cavity approximates an absorber; it does not force all radiation to one frequency.

options.t: The hole prevents the walls from reaching thermal equilibrium
options.why: A cavity at thermal equilibrium provides a stable setting in which blackbody radiation can be studied.

explain: A ray entering a small cavity opening undergoes many reflections; each reflection gives another chance of absorption. Only a small fraction escapes, so the opening behaves like an excellent absorber.

prompt: What did Planck's quantum hypothesis say about the energy of an oscillator of frequency f?

options.t: Its allowed energies occur in discrete amounts proportional to hf
It can have any energy continuously, independent of frequency
options.why: Planck introduced discrete energy elements proportional to frequency to account for the observed spectrum.

options.t: Its energy is always exactly h/f
options.why: The quantum energy is proportional to frequency: one quantum has energy hf.

options.t: Only the oscillator's temperature is quantized
options.why: Planck's proposal quantized the allowed oscillator energies, not temperature.

explain: Planck proposed that oscillator energies are quantized, with allowed values in multiples of hf (often written E_n=nhf). This resolved the classical prediction's failure for blackbody radiation.

prompt: As the temperature of a blackbody increases, how does the wavelength of peak emission change?

options.why: Wien's displacement law states that wavelength at peak emission is inversely proportional to absolute temperature.

options.t: It stays fixed because the material is unchanged
options.why: The peak wavelength depends on temperature even though the blackbody spectrum is independent of material.

options.t: It becomes zero at any finite temperature
options.why: The peak shifts toward shorter wavelengths as temperature rises but remains finite at finite temperature.

explain: Wien's displacement law is lambda_max T=b. Raising T therefore lowers the wavelength at which the spectrum peaks.

prompt: According to the Stefan-Boltzmann law, how does the power radiated per unit area by an ideal blackbody vary with absolute temperature?

options.why: The Stefan-Boltzmann law has a fourth-power dependence on absolute temperature.
The emitted power increases rapidly with temperature; it is not inversely proportional.
The total emitted power per unit area is sigma T^4 for an ideal blackbody.

explain: For an ideal blackbody the emitted power per unit area is P/A=sigma T^4, where sigma is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant.

prompt: What is the photoelectric effect?

options.t: Emission of electrons from a material when suitable-frequency radiation shines on it
Emission of photons when electrons are heated in a vacuum
options.why: In the photoelectric effect, light incident on a surface causes electrons to be emitted.

options.t: Reflection of all light from a metal surface
options.why: The effect concerns electron emission, not simply reflected light.

options.t: A change in an atom's nucleus caused by visible light
options.tag: Confused an electronic process with a nuclear one
options.why: Photoelectrons are emitted from the material's electronic structure; the process is not a nuclear reaction.

explain: In the photoelectric effect, incident radiation of suitable frequency transfers energy to electrons in a material, and some electrons escape from its surface.

prompt: A photon of frequency f has what energy?

options.why: Photon energy is directly proportional to frequency.
Planck's relation is linear in frequency: E=hf.
Multiplying frequency by Planck's constant gives the energy.

explain: The photon energy is E=hf, where h is Planck's constant. Since c=f lambda, higher frequency corresponds to shorter wavelength and greater photon energy.

prompt: For a metal with work function phi, what is the threshold frequency for photoemission?

options.why: At threshold, hf0=phi, so divide the work function by h.
The threshold follows directly from equating the photon energy hf0 to the work function.
Solving hf0=phi for f0 gives phi/h.

explain: At threshold the photon supplies exactly the work function: hf0=phi. Therefore f0=phi/h.

prompt: For light above the threshold frequency, which equation gives the maximum kinetic energy of an emitted photoelectron?

options.tag: Added the energy needed to escape
options.why: The work function is spent escaping the surface, leaving photon energy minus phi as kinetic energy.
For emission, hf is at least phi; the excess becomes the electron's kinetic energy.
The photon energy is hf, not h/f.

explain: Einstein's photoelectric equation is hf=phi+Kmax. The work function supplies the escape energy and the remainder becomes the maximum kinetic energy.

prompt: For light already above a metal's threshold frequency, what is the main effect of increasing its intensity while keeping its frequency fixed?

options.t: More photoelectrons are emitted per unit time, while their maximum kinetic energy is unchanged
The maximum kinetic energy rises because each photon has more energy
options.why: At fixed frequency, each photon still has energy hf; intensity mainly changes the photon flux.

options.t: Photoemission stops because the work function increases
options.tag: Made the material property depend on intensity
options.why: The work function is a property of the material and does not increase simply because light intensity is raised.

options.t: The threshold frequency falls to zero
options.why: Threshold frequency is determined by the work function, not by the incident intensity.

explain: At fixed frequency, increasing intensity increases the number of incident photons per unit time, and typically the emission rate. The energy per photon hf, and hence Kmax=hf-phi, is unchanged.

prompt: What is the stopping potential Vs related to the maximum photoelectron kinetic energy Kmax?

options.why: The stopping potential's energy is eVs, so divide kinetic energy by e to find Vs.
An electron's change in electric potential energy has magnitude eVs.
Potential difference times charge gives energy: Kmax=eVs.

explain: A retarding potential stops even the most energetic photoelectrons when eVs=Kmax, where e is the magnitude of the electron charge.

prompt: Why does the Bohr model produce discrete emission and absorption lines for hydrogen?

options.t: Electrons occupy allowed energy levels and photons carry the energy difference between levels
Electrons can have any orbit energy but emit only one fixed photon energy
options.why: The model quantizes allowed electron energies; transition energies are differences between those levels.

options.t: The nucleus emits a continuous range of electron energies
options.tag: Assigned the transition to the nucleus
options.why: In the Bohr model, spectral photons are emitted or absorbed during electron transitions between allowed states.

options.t: The atom's radius is fixed at every energy
options.why: The model allows different discrete orbits with different energies and radii.

explain: Only certain electron energies are allowed. A transition between two levels emits or absorbs a photon whose energy equals the difference, Delta E=hf, producing discrete spectral lines.

prompt: In the Bohr model, what happens when a hydrogen electron moves from a lower energy level to a higher one?

options.t: It absorbs a photon with energy equal to the level difference
It emits a photon and loses the level difference
options.why: Moving to a higher energy requires the atom to absorb energy; a downward transition emits a photon.

options.t: It emits a photon with an arbitrary energy
options.why: The photon energy must match the difference between the two allowed levels.

options.t: Its energy stays unchanged because the orbit is quantized
options.why: Quantization permits discrete energies; a transition between them changes the electron's energy.

explain: An upward transition requires energy input. The atom absorbs a photon whose energy equals the difference between the final and initial energy levels.

prompt: For hydrogen in the Bohr model, what is the energy of level n?

options.tag: Lost the negative sign and squared denominator
options.why: Bound hydrogen levels are negative and vary as 1/n^2.
The energy approaches zero from below as n increases; it is inversely proportional to n^2.
The ground state is -13.6 eV; higher levels have different, less negative energies.

explain: The Bohr energy levels of hydrogen are En=-13.6/n^2 eV. The negative sign indicates a bound state, and n=1 is the ground state.

prompt: A hydrogen atom's electron falls from n=3 to n=2. What is the emitted photon energy?

options.tag: Used the n=3 binding energy alone
options.why: The emitted photon energy is the difference between the n=3 and n=2 levels, not the energy of either level alone.

options.tag: Used the n=2 binding energy alone
options.why: The photon carries the difference between -1.51 eV and -3.40 eV.
Subtract the two level energies directly; there is no additional factor of one half.

explain: E3=-13.6/9=-1.51 eV and E2=-13.6/4=-3.40 eV. The emitted photon has energy E3-E2=1.89 eV.

prompt: Which quantization condition for angular momentum is used in the Bohr model?

options.t: L=n h/(2 pi)=n hbar, where n is a positive integer

options.why: The allowed angular momenta are integer multiples of hbar, not h divided by n.
The Bohr model assigns discrete, nonzero angular momenta to its allowed orbits.

options.tag: Used the wrong units and power
options.why: Angular momentum is quantized in units of hbar=h/(2pi), not h squared.

explain: Bohr's angular-momentum condition is L=n hbar=n h/(2pi), with n=1,2,3,... . It restricts the electron to particular allowed orbits.

prompt: What is the Bohr-model radius of the hydrogen orbit with principal quantum number n=3, in terms of the ground-state radius a0?

options.tag: Used a linear dependence on n
options.why: Bohr orbit radii scale as n^2, so the third orbit has radius 3^2 a0.
The radius grows with n^2; it is not inversely proportional to n^2.
The Bohr radius scales as the square of the principal quantum number.

explain: For hydrogen, the Bohr orbit radius is rn=n^2a0. At n=3, r3=9a0.

prompt: What is the de Broglie wavelength of a particle with momentum p?

options.why: The wavelength is inversely proportional to momentum.
Planck's constant divided by momentum has the units of length.
The de Broglie relation contains momentum to the first power.

explain: De Broglie's relation assigns a matter wavelength lambda=h/p to a particle of momentum p. For a nonrelativistic particle, p=mv.

prompt: An electron's momentum is doubled while its Planck constant remains the same. What happens to its de Broglie wavelength?

options.why: Because lambda=h/p, increasing momentum decreases wavelength inversely.
Matter wavelength depends inversely on the particle's momentum.
The wavelength varies as 1/p, not 1/p^2.

explain: With lambda=h/p, doubling p changes the wavelength to h/(2p), which is half its original value.

prompt: How does a standing matter wave around a Bohr orbit explain angular-momentum quantization?

options.t: The orbit circumference must contain an integer number of de Broglie wavelengths, giving 2 pi r=n lambda
The orbit must contain half a wavelength regardless of its radius
options.why: A stable circular standing wave requires an integer number of wavelengths around the circumference.

options.t: The wavelength must equal the orbit's diameter for every n
options.why: The number of wavelengths around the orbit is an integer n, so different n values give different allowed orbits.

options.t: The electron's momentum must vanish at the orbit
options.tag: Confused wave quantization with zero motion
options.why: The orbiting electron has nonzero momentum; its matter wavelength must fit consistently around the orbit.

explain: A stable circular matter wave must join smoothly after one orbit: 2pi r=n lambda. Substituting lambda=h/(mv) gives mvr=nh/(2pi)=n hbar, the Bohr angular-momentum condition.

prompt: What observation in the Davisson-Germer experiment supported de Broglie's matter-wave hypothesis?

options.t: Electrons scattered by a crystal produced a diffraction pattern
A heated metal emitted electrons below every threshold frequency
options.why: Davisson-Germer measured electron diffraction from a crystal, supporting the wave nature of electrons.

options.t: Hydrogen atoms emitted a continuous spectrum
options.why: The experiment concerned electron scattering and diffraction, not hydrogen emission spectra.

options.t: Light bent around a slit while electrons remained particle-like
options.why: The key evidence was the diffraction of electrons by a crystal lattice.

explain: Davisson and Germer observed diffraction of electrons by a crystal. The diffraction pattern is characteristic of waves and agreed with the electron wavelength predicted by de Broglie.

prompt: Which inequality expresses the position-momentum uncertainty principle?

options.tag: Assumed both quantities can be exact
options.why: Quantum mechanics imposes a nonzero lower bound on the product of the uncertainties.

options.tag: Used a ratio instead of a product
options.why: The uncertainty relation involves the product of position and momentum uncertainties.
The product cannot fall below hbar/2.

explain: Heisenberg's position-momentum relation is Delta x Delta p >= hbar/2. The two uncertainties cannot both be made arbitrarily small in the same quantum state.

prompt: If the position uncertainty of a particle is reduced, what must happen to its momentum uncertainty?

options.t: It must increase enough that Delta x Delta p remains at least hbar/2
It must also decrease to zero
options.tag: Tried to make incompatible uncertainties vanish together
options.why: The uncertainty product has a nonzero lower bound, so reducing one generally requires increasing the other.

options.t: It becomes exactly hbar/(2 Delta x) in every state
options.tag: Mistook a lower bound for an equality
options.why: The relation sets a minimum product; a particular state need not saturate the bound.

options.t: It stays constant for every possible state
options.why: The product is bounded below but can be larger than hbar/2.

explain: Since Delta x Delta p cannot be less than hbar/2, a smaller position uncertainty requires a sufficiently larger momentum uncertainty. The product can exceed, but not fall below, the bound.

prompt: Why is the uncertainty principle usually negligible for everyday macroscopic objects?

options.t: For their large masses, the corresponding velocity uncertainties are typically too small to notice
The uncertainty relation stops applying above atomic size
options.why: The relation still applies, but its effects are generally negligible at macroscopic scales.

options.tag: Confused small uncertainty with zero motion
options.why: Macroscopic objects can have substantial momentum; their relative quantum uncertainties are usually tiny.

options.t: Measurement removes all uncertainty for large objects
options.tag: Attributed the scale difference to perfect instruments
options.why: The principle is intrinsic to quantum states, not a limitation that disappears with better instruments.

explain: The uncertainty principle applies generally. For a macroscopic mass, a given momentum uncertainty corresponds to an extremely small velocity uncertainty, so the effect is usually unobservable in everyday motion.

prompt: Which statement best describes the quantum-mechanical uncertainty principle?

options.t: It is an intrinsic limit on jointly precise values of certain pairs of observables, such as position and momentum
It says every measurement device has a fixed calibration error
options.tag: Confused intrinsic uncertainty with instrument error
options.why: The uncertainty relation is a property of quantum states, not merely a defect in a measuring device.

options.t: It says particles have no definite state before measurement
options.why: The uncertainty relation constrains the spread of measurement outcomes; it is not simply a claim that no state exists.

options.t: It applies only when the particle is moving at the speed of light
options.why: The uncertainty principle applies to quantum systems regardless of whether they are relativistic.

explain: The uncertainty principle constrains the simultaneous statistical spreads of incompatible observables. It is not merely the result of imperfect measuring equipment.

prompt: In the wave-function description, what does |Psi(x,t)|^2 represent?

options.t: The probability density for finding the particle near position x at time t
The particle's electric charge at x
options.tag: Assigned the wave function a material property
options.why: The Born interpretation gives |Psi|^2 as probability density, not electric charge.

options.t: The probability amplitude itself, including its phase
options.why: Psi is the generally complex amplitude; its squared magnitude |Psi|^2 is the probability density.

options.tag: Confused a probability with a kinematic quantity
options.why: The wave function describes the quantum state; |Psi|^2 gives the position probability density.

explain: According to the Born interpretation, |Psi(x,t)|^2 is the probability density for position. Integrating it over a region gives the probability of finding the particle in that region.

prompt: What condition must a normalized one-dimensional wave function satisfy at a fixed time?

options.t: The integral of |Psi(x,t)|^2 over all space equals 1
The integral of Psi(x,t) over all space equals 0
options.tag: Normalized the amplitude rather than probability
options.why: Normalization requires total probability, the integral of |Psi|^2, to equal one.

options.t: Psi(x,t) must equal 1 at every position
options.tag: Confused normalization with a constant wave function
options.why: Normalization constrains the total probability, not the value of the wave function at every point.

options.t: The integral of |Psi(x,t)|^2 must equal the particle's mass
options.why: The total probability of finding the particle somewhere is one.

explain: For a normalized state, integral from -infinity to infinity of |Psi(x,t)|^2 dx=1. This ensures the total probability of finding the particle somewhere is one.

prompt: Which equation describes the time evolution of a quantum state in the time-dependent Schrödinger formulation?

options.t: H-hat Psi=i hbar partial Psi/partial t

options.why: The time-dependent Schrödinger equation relates the Hamiltonian acting on the state to its time derivative.

options.tag: Replaced an evolution equation with an algebraic identity
options.why: The equation is a differential equation in time, not a square relation.

options.t: partial Psi/partial t=i hbar H-hat Psi
options.tag: Inverted the factor of i hbar
options.why: Rearranging the standard equation gives partial Psi/partial t=H-hat Psi/(i hbar), not i hbar times H-hat Psi.

explain: The time-dependent Schrödinger equation is H-hat Psi=i hbar partial Psi/partial t. The Hamiltonian operator determines how the quantum state changes with time.

prompt: In quantum mechanics, how is a measurable observable such as energy represented?

options.t: By a complex probability with no associated operator
options.why: The quantum-mechanics postulates associate observables with linear Hermitian operators.

options.tag: Confused an observable with a frame change
options.why: Observables are represented by operators acting on states.

options.t: By an arbitrary nonlinear function of the wave function
options.why: The stated postulates use linear Hermitian operators for observables.

explain: The quantum postulates associate each classical observable with a linear Hermitian operator. Measurements yield eigenvalues of the corresponding operator.

prompt: If an observable operator satisfies A-hat psi=a psi, what measurement value is associated with this eigenstate?

options.tag: Reported the state instead of the observable value
options.why: The eigenvalue a is the measurable value associated with the eigenstate.

options.tag: Applied the operator again without reason
options.why: The eigenvalue equation already identifies the measurement value as a.
Eigenvalues can be nonzero and represent the possible measurement outcomes.

explain: An eigenstate of an observable's operator with eigenvalue a yields the value a when that observable is measured.

prompt: Why did quantum mechanics become necessary for describing atoms and subatomic particles?

options.t: Classical mechanics could not explain important observations at microscopic scales
Newtonian mechanics stopped working for planets
options.tag: Changed the scale of the problem
options.why: Classical mechanics remains highly useful for everyday and many astronomical systems; its limitations motivating quantum mechanics appeared at microscopic scales.

options.t: Quantum theory was introduced only to describe planetary orbits
options.tag: Applied quantum theory to the wrong domain
options.why: Quantum mechanics was developed to describe microscopic systems such as atoms and subatomic particles.

options.t: Classical mechanics could not describe any motion at all
options.why: Classical mechanics is successful in many regimes; quantum theory is needed where microscopic phenomena require it.

explain: Classical or Newtonian mechanics successfully describes many macroscopic phenomena but fails to account for observations involving atoms and subatomic particles. Quantum mechanics was developed to describe those microscopic systems.

prompt: Which statement captures wave-particle duality as used in modern physics?

options.t: Radiation and matter can show both wave-like and particle-like behavior in appropriate experiments
Only light can show wave behavior and only matter can show particle behavior
options.why: Both light and matter can display wave-like and particle-like properties, depending on how they interact or are measured.

options.t: Every particle always follows a visible classical wave path
options.tag: Treated a matter wave as a material ripple
options.why: Wave-particle duality describes quantum behavior; it does not mean a particle is a tiny classical wave in space.

options.t: Wave behavior and particle behavior occur only at the same time in every measurement
options.why: Different experiments reveal different aspects of quantum systems.

explain: Modern quantum theory describes light and matter using both wave-like and particle-like aspects. The behavior revealed depends on the physical interaction and measurement.

prompt: Which relation connects a photon's energy E to its frequency f?

options.why: Photon energy is Planck's constant times frequency; c relates frequency to wavelength, not energy in this expression.
Photon energy increases with frequency according to E=hf.

options.tag: Changed both the power and the ratio
options.why: The photon energy relation is linear in f and proportional to h.

explain: A photon has energy E=hf, where h is Planck's constant. This quantized relation underlies the photon explanation of the photoelectric effect.

prompt: Which pair gives the Lorentz transformation from K to K' when K' moves at speed v along the positive x direction?

options.why: The Galilean equations are the low-speed approximation; the Lorentz transformation includes gamma and mixes space with time.

options.tag: Used the opposite direction of motion
options.why: For K' moving in the positive x direction, the forward transformation uses minus signs.
The Lorentz transformation includes terms involving both v and the other coordinate.

explain: For relative motion along x, the Lorentz transformation is x'=gamma(x-vt) and t'=gamma(t-vx/c^2), with y'=y and z'=z.

prompt: An object has velocity u' along the x-axis in K', while K' moves at velocity v relative to K. Which formula gives the object's velocity in K?

options.t: u=u'+v with no correction at any speed
options.tag: Used Galilean addition at relativistic speeds
options.why: Relativistic velocity addition includes the denominator 1+u'v/c^2.
For the stated direction, combine u' and v with plus signs in both parts of the formula.
For velocities in the same positive direction, the denominator is 1+u'v/c^2.

explain: For collinear velocities, u=(u'+v)/(1+u'v/c^2). When both speeds are much smaller than c, the denominator is approximately one and the formula approaches Galilean addition.

prompt: A probe moves at 0.60c relative to a spacecraft, which moves at 0.50c relative to Earth in the same direction. What is the probe's speed relative to Earth?

options.tag: Added speeds using the Galilean rule
options.why: Relativistic velocity addition keeps the resulting speed below c.
The collinear velocity-addition law uses a sum divided by 1+u'v/c^2.
The denominator is 1+(0.60)(0.50)=1.30, so divide 1.10c by 1.30.

explain: u=(0.60c+0.50c)/(1+0.60*0.50)=1.10c/1.30=0.846c. Direct addition would incorrectly give a speed above c.

prompt: According to the relativistic velocity-addition law, what speed does an observer measure for a light pulse moving in the same direction as the observer's frame?

options.why: Relativistic velocity addition preserves the same vacuum light speed for every inertial observer.
The Lorentz transformation does not make an inertial observer measure a different vacuum light speed.

options.tag: Kept only part of the addition formula
options.why: Substituting u'=c into the full formula gives c exactly.

explain: Putting u'=c into u=(u'+v)/(1+u'v/c^2) gives u=(c+v)/(1+v/c)=c. This illustrates the invariance of the speed of light.

prompt: A blackbody is at 3000 K. Using Wien's constant 2.898 x 10^-3 m K, estimate the wavelength of peak emission.

options.why: Wien's law gives lambda_max=b/T, so divide the constant by the absolute temperature.

options.tag: Lost a factor of one thousand
Reported the temperature as a wavelength
options.why: Convert the temperature through lambda_max T=b; the peak is in the infrared for this temperature.

explain: Wien's law is lambda_max=b/T. Thus lambda_max=(2.898 x 10^-3)/(3000)=9.66 x 10^-7 m.

prompt: What was the ultraviolet catastrophe associated with the classical Rayleigh-Jeans prediction?

options.t: It predicted unbounded spectral energy at very short wavelengths, unlike observed blackbody spectra
It predicted zero radiation at every wavelength
options.why: The classical prediction became unphysical at short wavelengths by diverging rather than vanishing.

options.t: It predicted the peak wavelength was independent of temperature
options.tag: Confused the Wien-law observation with the catastrophe
options.why: The problem was the short-wavelength divergence of the classical spectrum.

options.t: It predicted atoms could emit only one wavelength
options.tag: Confused a continuous spectrum with line spectra
options.why: The classical blackbody calculation predicted too much radiation at high frequency, not a single spectral line.

explain: The Rayleigh-Jeans law agrees with measurements at long wavelengths but diverges at short wavelengths, predicting an infinite total radiated energy. Planck's quantized oscillator energies produce a finite spectrum consistent with observations.

prompt: What did Compton scattering reveal about a high-energy photon colliding with an electron?

options.t: The scattered photon can have a longer wavelength because energy and momentum are transferred to the electron
The photon always keeps exactly the same wavelength after scattering
options.why: Compton observed a wavelength shift, showing that the photon transfers energy and momentum in a collision.

options.t: The photon is absorbed and the electron's rest mass disappears
options.why: The photon and electron scatter; energy and momentum are conserved in the interaction.

options.t: The scattered photon has a shorter wavelength for every collision
options.why: For the described photon-electron scattering, the Compton shift is nonnegative and depends on angle; forward scattering has zero shift.

explain: In Compton scattering, a photon transfers energy and momentum to an electron. The scattered photon generally has lower energy and therefore a longer wavelength; the shift depends on scattering angle.

prompt: Which expression gives the Compton wavelength shift when a photon scatters through angle theta from an initially stationary electron?

options.why: The Compton shift is proportional to 1-cos(theta); it vanishes for forward scattering.
The electron Compton wavelength is h/(m_e c), not m_e c/h.
The change is the difference between initial and scattered wavelengths, giving the factor 1-cos(theta).

explain: The Compton formula is lambda'-lambda=(h/(m_e c))(1-cos theta). It follows from conserving energy and momentum in a photon-electron collision.

prompt: A metal has work function 2.3 eV and is illuminated with 200 nm light. Approximately what is the maximum photoelectron speed? Use hc=1240 eV nm and m_e=9.11 x 10^-31 kg.

options.tag: Used the full photon energy as kinetic energy
options.why: Subtract the 2.3 eV work function from the 6.2 eV photon energy before finding the speed.

options.tag: Used half the available kinetic energy
options.why: The photoelectron has Kmax=6.2-2.3=3.9 eV; then use K=mv^2/2.

options.tag: Used kinetic energy as a speed
options.why: Convert 3.9 eV to joules and solve v=sqrt(2K/m).

explain: The photon energy is 1240/200=6.2 eV, so Kmax=6.2-2.3=3.9 eV=6.25 x 10^-19 J. Therefore v=sqrt(2K/m_e)=1.17 x 10^6 m/s.

prompt: In the Bohr model, what is the ground-state energy of a hydrogen-like ion with nuclear charge Z?

options.why: For a one-electron hydrogen-like ion, the Coulomb binding energy scales as Z squared.
A larger nuclear charge binds the electron more strongly, increasing the magnitude of the ground-state energy by Z^2.
Bound-state energies are negative when the zero of energy is defined at infinite separation.

explain: For a hydrogen-like ion, En=-13.6 Z^2/n^2 eV. Setting n=1 gives the ground-state energy -13.6 Z^2 eV.

prompt: A nonrelativistic electron has kinetic energy 4.0 eV. Approximately what is its de Broglie wavelength? Use lambda(nm)=1.227/sqrt(K in eV).

options.tag: Multiplied by the square root of energy
options.why: For a nonrelativistic electron, wavelength is inversely proportional to the square root of kinetic energy.

options.tag: Used twice the energy in the square root
options.why: Substitute K=4.0 eV into 1.227/sqrt(K), which gives 1.227/2 nm.

options.tag: Divided by energy instead of its square root
options.why: The momentum is proportional to sqrt(K), so lambda varies as 1/sqrt(K).

explain: For a nonrelativistic electron, p=sqrt(2m_e K) and lambda=h/p. Using the supplied conversion gives lambda=1.227/sqrt(4.0)=0.614 nm.

prompt: An electron has kinetic energy 50 keV, comparable to its rest energy. Which momentum relation should be used to calculate its de Broglie wavelength?

options.t: p=sqrt(2m_e K) without checking the speed
options.why: At kinetic energies that are a significant fraction of the electron rest energy, the relativistic energy-momentum relation is needed.

options.tag: Confused photon momentum with massive-particle momentum
options.why: For a massive particle with kinetic energy K, use the relativistic energy-momentum relation; p=E/c applies to a photon.

options.tag: Used a wavelength directly proportional to momentum
options.why: Once p is determined, the de Broglie relation is lambda=h/p.

explain: For relativistic kinetic energy K and rest energy m_e c^2, p c=sqrt(K(K+2m_e c^2)). The wavelength is then lambda=h/p; the nonrelativistic formula is not accurate when K is a substantial fraction of the rest energy.

prompt: An electron's position is known to within 0.050 nm. What is the minimum uncertainty in its velocity from Delta x Delta p >= hbar/2? Use m_e=9.11 x 10^-31 kg and hbar=1.055 x 10^-34 J s.

options.tag: Omitted the factor of two in the uncertainty bound
options.why: The lower bound is hbar/(2 Delta x m_e), not hbar/(4 Delta x m_e).
0.050 nm is 5.0 x 10^-11 m; using this SI value gives about 1.16 x 10^6 m/s.

options.tag: Used h instead of hbar in the stated bound
options.why: The supplied relation uses hbar/2, which is h/(4 pi), not h/2.

explain: For a nonrelativistic electron, Delta p=m_e Delta v, so Delta v >= hbar/(2m_e Delta x). With Delta x=5.0 x 10^-11 m, the minimum is approximately 1.16 x 10^6 m/s.

prompt: An excited state has a lifetime uncertainty of 2.0 x 10^-6 s. Using Delta E Delta t >= hbar/2, what is the minimum energy uncertainty in eV? Use hbar=1.055 x 10^-34 J s and 1 eV=1.602 x 10^-19 J.

options.why: The specified lower bound is hbar/(2 Delta t), so halve hbar/Delta t.
Convert joules to eV by dividing by 1.602 x 10^-19 J/eV.
Dividing hbar by a microsecond-scale lifetime gives an energy of order 10^-29 J, not 10^-23 J.

explain: Delta E_min=hbar/(2 Delta t)=1.055 x 10^-34/(4.0 x 10^-6)=2.64 x 10^-29 J. Dividing by 1.602 x 10^-19 J/eV gives 1.65 x 10^-10 eV.

prompt: What is the frequency of the photon emitted when hydrogen falls from n=2 to n=1? Use the level energies -13.6/n^2 eV and h=4.136 x 10^-15 eV s.

options.tag: Used the n=1 binding energy as the photon energy
options.why: The photon energy is the difference between the initial and final levels, 10.2 eV, not 13.6 eV.

options.tag: Used the energy of the n=2 level alone
options.why: The transition energy is 13.6-3.4=10.2 eV.
Since E=hf, frequency is E/h, not h/E.

explain: The levels are E1=-13.6 eV and E2=-3.40 eV, so the photon energy is 10.2 eV. The frequency is f=Delta E/h=10.2/(4.136 x 10^-15)=2.47 x 10^15 Hz.
